common_name: Star of Toscane Yellow Star Jasmine

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring against a trellis, fence, or wall in fertile, well-drained soil; this compact selection takes a season or two to establish before putting on strong twining growth.

directions: Star of Toscane is a sport of common star jasmine distinguished by flowers that open creamy white and mature to a soft golden yellow, a departure from the pure white blooms of the species, carried amid the same glossy, narrow, leathery leaves that often bronze in winter cold. Grow it in full sun to partial shade in neutral, fertile, well-drained soil against a trellis, fence, or wall, where its twining stems need tying support since it does not cling like a true clinging vine. It flowers from early summer into autumn with the same heady, sweet fragrance typical of the genus, and is more compact and restrained in habit than the straight species, making it a better fit for smaller garden structures. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce once mature, as the plant is reasonably drought tolerant. Prune after flowering only as needed to shape or control size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a trellis or sunny wall in well-drained soil; in colder zones it is also grown in containers that can be moved to shelter for winter.

directions: Flame is a variegated star jasmine selection prized for foliage that flushes pink to red in cool weather against cream-margined green leaves, giving strong color interest even outside the fragrant white pinwheel-flower season. Grow it on a trellis, obelisk, or fence in part shade to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and keep it evenly moist while young. The coloring intensifies with cooler temperatures and bright light, so a spot with some direct sun brings out the best red tones. Prune lightly after the main summer flowering flush to maintain shape and encourage branching; in regions at the cold edge of its range it benefits from a sheltered microclimate or winter protection.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring against a shaded wall, tree trunk, or sturdy trellis in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; expect a slow start while the vine establishes aerial rootlets before it begins climbing in earnest.

directions: Rose Sensation bears flattened lacecap flowerheads in June and July with marbled, rose-pink sterile sepals surrounding the tiny fertile flowers, a strong color departure from the usual white-bracted Schizophragma hydrangeoides. Deep green, ovate, toothed leaves turn rich yellow in fall. It climbs by self-clinging aerial rootlets once established and makes an outstanding choice for a north-facing or otherwise shaded wall, though flowering is best with at least some direct sun. Young plants may need temporary tying to their support until the aerial roots take hold; after that, no staking or pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood after bloom, since flowers form on old wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; good fall color develops best with some direct sun.

directions: Sold under the trade name Red Wall, this selection of native Virginia creeper is grown for an especially showy and consistent seasonal foliage progression: new leaves open with bronze tones in early spring, mature to solid dark green through summer, then turn a vivid fire-engine red in fall, a more reliable and vivid display than many unselected seedlings. It clings tightly to brick, stone, wood, and other masonry surfaces with adhesive tendril discs, tolerating poor soil, drought, shade, and urban pollution like the species. Dark blue berries that follow feed birds into winter, and the foliage hosts several native moth species. Prune to keep growth off windows, gutters, and shingles, since the adhesive discs can mark some surfaces and are difficult to remove once attached.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils.

directions: Yellow Wall is a Virginia creeper selection grown for its buttery golden-yellow autumn foliage, a departure from the familiar scarlet fall color of the typical species, though the display is often briefer than the red-turning forms. Summer foliage is the same palmate, five-lobed, deep green typical of the species. It self-clings to brick, stone, and wood with adhesive tendril discs, is extremely tough and adaptable to poor soil, drought, shade, and urban pollution, and provides dark blue berries valuable to birds in fall. Prune to keep growth off windows, gutters, and shingles where the adhesive discs can damage surfaces.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a modest trellis or obelisk; its compact habit suits smaller supports than the vigorous straight species.

directions: Purple Bouquet is a compact selection of chocolate vine that reaches roughly half the size of the straight species, making it a better fit for smaller trellises, obelisks, and mailbox posts rather than large pergolas. It bears the same chocolate-scented, mauve-purple flower clusters in spring on fine-textured, five-fingered foliage, and like other Akebia quinata selections it sets its unusual sausage-shaped, sweet-pulped fruit best when a second, genetically distinct plant is grown nearby for cross-pollination. Grow it in partial shade to full sun in average, well-drained soil, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain its tidy habit, since it is considerably less rampant than unselected chocolate vine.
